title: Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids
statement: Each entry `cuboids[i] = [width, length, height]` describes a box. Pick any subset of the boxes and build a single tower from them, where every box may be rotated freely so its three measurements are assigned to width, length and height in any order. A box may sit directly on another only if, after rotation, none of its three measurements (width, length, height) is larger than the matching measurement of the box below. Return the greatest total height such a tower can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every subset in every order and rotation explodes quickly. The key observation: if a box can go on top of another in some orientation, it still can when both are turned so their measurements are sorted (smallest as width, largest as height). Sorted measurements pair up in order, so if box a can sit on box b in any arrangement, a's sorted triple is component-wise at most b's. Putting the largest side up also maximises each box's contribution. Once every box is normalised this way and the boxes are sorted, a valid tower is just a chain of boxes that grow in all three measurements, so the problem becomes a longest-increasing-subsequence style DP that maximises the sum of heights.

## Approach

1. Sort each cuboid's measurements so `[small, middle, large]` and treat `large` as its height.
2. Sort the boxes lexicographically; any box that can go below another then comes later.
3. `dp[i]` is the tallest tower whose bottom box is `boxes[i]`: start with its own height.
4. For every earlier `j` whose three measurements are all at most those of `i`, try `dp[j] + boxes[i][2]`.
5. Track the best `dp[i]` in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

Normalised boxes: `[20, 45, 50]`, `[37, 53, 95]`, `[12, 23, 45]`. Sorted: `[12, 23, 45]`, `[20, 45, 50]`, `[37, 53, 95]`.

- `dp[0] = 45`.
- `dp[1]`: box 0 fits, so `45 + 50 = 95`.
- `dp[2]`: both fit; the better is `dp[1] + 95 = 190`.

`best = 190`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every pair of boxes is compared once after an O(n log n) sort.
- Space: O(n) for the normalised boxes and `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- Checking only width and length is wrong: the height of the upper box may not exceed the lower one's either.
- Sorting the boxes is what makes `j < i` cover every possible box above `i`; equal boxes are fine because `<=` allows stacking duplicates.
- Turning only the largest side up while leaving width and length unsorted makes the fit check miss valid placements; sort all three measurements.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `boxes` | cuboids with sorted measurements, sorted lexicographically |
| `dp[i]` | tallest tower that has `boxes[i]` at the bottom |
| `i`, `j` | the bottom box and a candidate box resting on it |
| `fits` | whether `boxes[j]` can sit on `boxes[i]` |
| `best` | tallest tower found so far |

narration.2: Sort each box's measurements so its largest side becomes the height.
narration.3: Order the boxes so any box that can rest on another comes before it.
narration.4: dp[i] will hold the tallest tower with box i at the bottom.
narration.7: Consider each box as the bottom of a tower.
narration.8: On its own, the box gives a tower as tall as its height.
narration.9: Look at every earlier box as the one directly above it.
narration.10: Box j can sit on box i only if none of its three measurements is larger.
narration.12: Stack the best tower ending at j on top of box i if that is taller.
narration.15: Remember the tallest tower seen so far.
narration.17: Return the tallest tower over all bottom boxes.
